name: introduction_1
content: This wave climate report presents wave information for {locName} in {cntName}. This report contains information about wind-generated surface gravity waves, often called wind waves and swell. The wave climate is defined here as the statistics of waves conditions over a {hindcastDuration} years period. The report details the average wave conditions (Page X), the variability of wave conditions (Page X), severe and extreme waves (Page X) and characterises the wave energy resource (Page X). Similar wave climate reports are available for more than 200 locations around the Pacific, near important ports, large settlements, tide gauge locations and areas where the wave climate is of particular interest. Other locations in {cntName} are shown in Figure 1 (Front Page). Because little wave data exists for the Pacific, the information presented here was derived from a computer model: a regional wave hindcast.

name: introduction_2
content: The wave hindcast evaluated the wave conditions in the region between {yearStart} and {yearEnd}. The hindcast was produced by the Centre for Australian Weather and Climate Research, and updated by the Bureau of Meteorology (Australia) since 2013 onwards and focusses on the central and South Pacific with a resolution of 10 to 4 arcminutes (~20 to 8km) and therefore is accurate for offshore wave conditions. The model was constrained by the best available data and thoroughly verified against waves measurements. In the Pacific region, the wave hindcast produced resonably good results with an average skill of 0.85 (skills between 0.8 and 0.9 are considered good, above 0.9 is considered excellent, (see Table 1). For more information about the regional wave hindcast, readers should refer to Durrant et al. (2014) and Smith et al. (2020). This report was generated by a computer program created at SPC-Geoscience which analysed the output from the wave hindcast and summarised the findings. Therefore, despite our best effort, this report may contain errors and ommissions and should be used with caution.

name: averageWaveConditions_1
content: Wave condition is usually defined by the significant wave height, the peak period and the peak direction. The significant wave height is defined as the mean wave height (from trough to crest) of the highest third of the waves and correspond to the wave height that would be reported by an experienced observer. The peak period is the time interval between two waves of the dominant waves. The peak direction is the direction the dominant waves are coming from. Note that this document uses the nautical convention and therefore reports the direction the waves (or wind) are coming from, measured positively clockwise from geographic North.

name: averageWaveConditions_2
content: This page provides information about the average wave climate of {locName} in {cntName}. The average sea state is {avgWave_seaState}, dominated by {avgWave_waveType}. The annual mean wave height is {avgWave_meanHs:.2f} meters, the annual mean wave direction is {avgWave_meanDp:.0f}° and the annual mean wave period is {avgWave_meanTp:.2f} seconds. Table 2 summarize the mean wave condition for {locName}.

name: averageWaveConditions_3
content: In the Pacific, waves often comes from multiple directions and with different periods at a time. In {locName}, there are often more than {avgWave_nComponents:.0f} different wave direction/period components. Wave conditions tend to be consistent, meaning that they vary little within a few hours. The mean annual and seasonal variability are reported in Table 2. For more information on the wave climate variability refer to Page X.

name: meanWaveRose_1
content: The mean wave condition, does not describe the variety of wave heights and directions that can occur in {locName}. A better representation of the variety of waves is the wave rose (Figure 2). The annual wave rose shows where waves usually come from and the size of waves associated with each direction. It is a powerful illustration of the distribution of wave heights and directions. The circles (polar axis) represent how often a wave direction/height occurs (i.e. the percentage of occurrence); each circle shows the 10% occurrence. Each wedge represents a range of directions 20 degrees wide <font color="red">with the center direction of each wedge</font> displayed on the outer circle. Wave heights are split into intervals of 0.25m. Each interval is associated with a colour on the color-scale right off the rose

name: meanWaveRose_2
content: {meanWaRose_waveHistory} {meanWaRose_seaState} Waves principaly came from the {meanWaRose_Dirp}.

name: waveVariation_1
content: The wave climate is rarely constant throughout the year and seasonal changes in wind patterns across the Pacific Ocean can greatly modify the wave conditions from one season to the next. This page provides a description of these variations in {locName}. The monthly variability (or coefficient of variation) of the wave height is used to quantify these variations, in {locName} the variability of the wave height is {waveVar_HsVarCoeff:.1f}%. Typically, locations that are mostly exposed to trade winds show the smallest variation (less than 25%). Locations exposed to the Southern Ocean swell show larger monthly variation (between 25 and 30%) and locations exposed to the North Pacific swell show the largest monthly variation (>30%). The monthly variability gives an idea of how the wave condition changes from one month to the next but to better understand the seasonal changes requires to look at the seasonal wave roses (Figure 3).

name: waveVariation_2
content: {waveVar_summerSeaState} The principal wave direction is from the {waveVar_summerDirp}. {waveVar_autumnSeaState} The principal wave direction is from the {waveVar_autumnDirp}. {waveVar_winterSeaState} The principal wave direction is from the {waveVar_winterDirp}. {waveVar_springSeaState} The principal wave direction is from the {waveVar_springDirp}.

name: waveVariation_3
content: The monthly wave height, period and direction show the seasonal changes in the wave parameters with more details on the transition between seasons. The average wave height during calm periods (10% of the lowest wave height) and large swell events (10% of the largest wave heights) also changes with seasons. Figure 4 can help in finding the best month for servicing or installing offshore structures and moorings

name: waveVariation_4
content: Waves change from month to month with the seasons but they also change from year to year with climate oscillations. Typically these changes are smaller than the seasonal changes but can be important during phenomenon such as El Niño. In {locName}, the inter-annual variability (or coefficient of variation) for wave height is {waveVar_HsVarCoeff_InterAnnual:.1f}%, the average variability for the Pacific Region is typically 7%. In {locName} the mean annual wave height has {waveVar_HsTrend} since 1979. The mean annual wave height in {locName} is {waveVar_CorrClimate}. The 1997/1998 El Niño greatly affected the wave climate in the Pacific region and in most islands a dramatric change in the wave patterns could be observed (Figure 5)

name: largeSevereWaves_1
content: From time to time the waves become larger to a point where they can cause erosion of the beaches and inundation of the shore. Large waves are waves that exceed the 90th percentile of the waveheight. In other words large wave occur 10% of the time (37 days in a year). Large wave are typically the largest event expected each month. Large wave rarely cause damage on the coast or inundation but water activities during large wave events can be hazardous. Large wave events do cause coastal inundation and erosion when they occur at the same time than large spring tide such as perigean spring tides (also called king tides). In {locName} the threshold for large waves is {severeWave_thresholdLarge:.2f} meters.

name: largeSevereWaves_2
content: Severe waves are less common than large waves. They are the waves that occur less than 1% of the time (4 days in a year). Severe waves typically occur once or twice in a year. Severe waves can be associated with coastal erosion and inundations especially if they occur during spring tides and water activities are hazardous on the coast during these events. In {locName} the threshold for severe waves is {severeWave_thresholdSevere:.2f} meters.

name: largeSevereWaves_3
content: Large and severe waves can be generated by different weather events such as, cyclones, distant extra tropical storms and fresh trade winds. The direction and period of the waves are telltale of the origin of the large waves. This information can be derived from the large, severe and extreme wave rose (Figure 6). In {locName}, the dominant direction for wave height larger than {severeWave_thresholdLarge:.2f} meters is from the {severeWave_Dirp}.

name: largeSevereWaves_4
content: Larger waves can be generated by different meteorological phenomena such as tropical cyclones, extra-tropical storm or fresh trade wind events. These meteorological events are very dependent on the seasons and so are the large waves. In {locName} large waves are bigger in {severeWave_mainSeason}. Large waves are also present during other seasons and the monthly variability of the large wave threshold (90th percentiles) for {locName} is {severeWave_monthlyVarCoeff:.2f}% (Figure 7). As mean wave height varies from year to year so does the larger waves. In {locName} the annual variability for the large wave threshold is {severeWave_yearlyVarCoeff:.2f}% (Figure 8).

name: extremeWaves_1
content: A list of the 30 largest wave events is presented in Table 3 with their ranking, date, wave height, wave period and direction at the peak of the event. The largest event that reached {locName} since {yearStart} was on {extremeWave_largestDate} and exceeded {extremeWave_largestHs:.0f} meters which is considered {extremeWave_largestCondition}. All the listed events have a wave height higher than {extremeWave_smallestHs:.0f} meter which is considered {extremeWave_smallestCondition}. The list of the 30 largest events can be used to calculate the probability of occurrence of wave event larger than the average largest annual wave height. Such analysis, called an extreme wave analysis, is presented in the next page.

name: extremeWaves_2
content: Extreme wave analysis are used to assess the probability of occurrence of wave events larger than the severe wave height. It is often used to evaluate the vulnerability of communities to coastal inundation and to decide how high a seawall or a jetty needs to be built. Extreme wave analysis is a statistical analysis that looks at the distribution of past wave events and extrapolates (predict) the probability of occurrence of unusually large events that may have never been recorded. The probability of an event to occur within a year is often presented as an Annual Return Interval (ARI). The ARI is the probability of an event to occur within a year. For example the probability of a 100 year ARI event to occur within any given year is 1%. Similarly the probability of a 50 year ARI event to occur within any given year is 2%.

name: extremeWaves_3
content: The analysis completed for {locName} was done by defining a threshold of severe heights and fitting a Generalised Pareto Distribution (hereafter GPD). The optimum threshold was selected at {extremeWave_EVA_threshold:.2f} meters. In the {hindcastDuration} years wave hindcast, {extremeWave_EVA_nEvents} wave events have reached or exceeded this threshold. The GPD was fitted to the largest wave height reached during each of these events (Figure 9). Extreme wave analyses are a very useful tool but are not always accurate because the analysis is very sensitive to the data available, the type of distribution fitted and the threshold used. For example, this analysis does not accurately account for Tropical Cyclone waves. More in-depth analysis is required to obtain results fit for designing coastal infrastructures and coastal hazards planning.

name: wind_1
content: Wind is the origin of all waves and although swells are created by distant wind events, local winds can significantly affect the local waves. In {locName} the prevailing wind is dominated by {wind_tradeWinds} with a mean wind speed of {wind_wSpeed:.2f} m/s ({wind_wSpeedKnots:.2f} knots) from the {wind_Dirp}. Figure 11 shows the wind rose for {locName} and Figure 12 shows the monthly mean wind speed and direction. Note that the results presented here use the nautical convention: directions shown are the directions the wind is blowing from.
